items.new: Call me Ishmael. Some years ago — never mind how long exactly — having little or no money in my purse, and nothing in particular to interest me on shore, I thought I would sail around a little and see the watery part of the world. It's a way I have of driving off the blues and regulating my circulation. Whenever I find myself growing grim about the mouth; whenever it is a damp, drizzly November in my soul; whenever I find myself involuntarily pausing in front of coffin warehouses, and bringing up the rear of every funeral I meet; and especially whenever my low spirits get such an upper hand over me that it takes a strong moral principle to keep me from deliberately stepping into the street and methodically knocking people's hats off — then I consider it high time to get to sea as soon as I can. This is my substitute for pistol and bullet. With a philosophical flourish Cato throws himself on his sword; I quietly take to the ship. There is nothing surprising in this. If they only knew it, almost all men in their degree, at some time or other, cherish very nearly the same feelings toward the ocean as I do.

Nothing will satisfy them but the very outermost edge of the land; loitering in the shady lee of those warehouses over there won't do. Tell me, does the magnetic power of the compass needles of all those ships draw them here?

items.new: But here is an artist. He wants to paint you the dreamiest, shadiest, quietest, most enchanting bit of romantic landscape in all the valley of the Saco. What is the chief element he uses? There stand his trees, each with a hollow trunk, as if a hermit and a crucifix were inside; and here sleeps his meadow, and there sleep his cattle; and up from that cottage over there rises a sleepy smoke. Deep into distant woodlands winds a mazy path, reaching to overlapping spurs of mountains bathed in their hillside blue. But though the picture lies entranced like this, and though this pine tree shakes down its sighs like leaves upon this shepherd's head, it would all be in vain unless the shepherd's eye were fixed on the magic stream before him. Go visit the Prairies in June, when for scores upon scores of miles you wade knee-deep among tiger lilies — what is the one charm missing? Water — there is not a drop of water there! If Niagara were only a cataract of sand, would you travel your thousand miles to see it? Why did the poor poet of Tennessee, on suddenly receiving two handfuls of silver, debate whether to buy himself a coat, which he sadly needed, or invest his money in a walking trip to Rockaway Beach? Why is almost every robust, healthy boy with a robust, healthy soul in him at some time or other crazy to go to sea? Why, on your first voyage as a passenger, did you yourself feel such a mystical vibration when first told that you and your ship were now out of sight of land? Why did the old Persians hold the sea holy? Why did the Greeks give it a separate god, and own brother of Jove? Surely all this is not without meaning. And still deeper is the meaning of that story of Narcissus, who, because he could not grasp the tormenting, mild image he saw in the fountain, plunged into it and was drowned. But that same image we ourselves see in all rivers and oceans. It is the image of the ungraspable phantom of life; and this is the key to it all.

items.new: Again, I always go to sea as a sailor because they make a point of paying me for my trouble, whereas they never pay passengers a single penny that I ever heard of. On the contrary, passengers themselves must pay. And there is all the difference in the world between paying and being paid. The act of paying is perhaps the most uncomfortable punishment that the two orchard thieves, Adam and Eve, brought down on us. But being paid — what can compare with that? The polished eagerness with which a man receives money is really marvelous, considering that we so earnestly believe money to be the root of all earthly ills, and that on no account can a moneyed man enter heaven. Ah! How cheerfully we consign ourselves to damnation!

items.new: Finally, I always go to sea as a sailor because of the healthy exercise and pure air of the forecastle deck. For as in this world headwinds are far more common than winds from astern (that is, if you never violate the Pythagorean maxim), so for the most part the Commodore on the quarterdeck gets his air secondhand from the sailors on the forecastle. He thinks he breathes it first; but not so. In much the same way the common people lead their leaders in many other things, while the leaders little suspect it. items.new: Chief among these motives was the overwhelming idea of the great whale himself. Such a portentous and mysterious monster roused all my curiosity. Then there were the wild and distant seas where he rolled his island bulk; the unspeakable, nameless perils of the whale; these, with all the accompanying marvels of a thousand Patagonian sights and sounds, helped to sway me to my wish. With other men, perhaps, such things would not have been temptations; but as for me, I am tormented by an everlasting itch for things remote. I love to sail forbidden seas and land on barbarous coasts. Not ignoring what is good, I am quick to perceive a horror, and could still be sociable with it — if they would let me — since it is only wise to be on friendly terms with all the inmates of the place one lodges in.

items.new: Since most young candidates for the pains and penalties of whaling stop at this same New Bedford, to embark on their voyage from there, I may as well say that I, for one, had no intention of doing so. My mind was made up to sail in nothing but a Nantucket craft, because there was a fine, boisterous something about everything connected with that famous old island that pleased me amazingly. Besides, though New Bedford has lately been gradually monopolizing the whaling business, and though poor old Nantucket is now far behind her in this matter, Nantucket was her great original — the Tyre of this Carthage — the place where the first dead American whale was stranded. Where else but from Nantucket did those aboriginal whalemen, the Red-Men, first sally out in canoes to give chase to the Leviathan? And where but from Nantucket, too, did that first adventurous little sloop set out, partly loaded with imported cobblestones — so the story goes — to throw at the whales, in order to find out when they were near enough to risk a harpoon from the bowsprit?

items.new: Now, with a night, a day, and still another night ahead of me in New Bedford before I could embark for my intended port, the question of where I was to eat and sleep in the meantime became a matter of concern. It was a very dubious-looking — no, a very dark and dismal — night, bitingly cold and cheerless. I knew no one in the place. With anxious grappling hooks I had sounded my pocket, and brought up only a few pieces of silver. So, wherever you go, Ishmael, I said to myself, as I stood in the middle of a dreary street shouldering my bag and comparing the gloom to the north with the darkness to the south — wherever in your wisdom you may decide to lodge for the night, my dear Ishmael, be sure to ask the price, and don't be too particular.

items.new: It was an odd sort of place — a gable-ended old house, one side palsied, as it were, and leaning over sadly. It stood on a sharp, bleak corner, where that tempestuous wind Euroclydon kept up a worse howling than it ever did around poor Paul's storm-tossed ship. Euroclydon, nevertheless, is a mighty pleasant breeze to anyone indoors, with his feet on the hearth, quietly toasting them before bed. "In judging of that tempestuous wind called Euroclydon," says an old writer — of whose works I possess the only surviving copy — "it makes a marvelous difference whether you look out at it from a glass window where the frost is all on the outside, or whether you observe it from that sashless window, where the frost is on both sides, and of which that fellow Death is the only glazier." True enough, I thought, as this passage came to mind — old black-letter, you reason well. Yes, these eyes are windows, and this body of mine is the house. What a pity they didn't stop up the chinks and crannies, though, and stuff in a little lint here and there. But it's too late to make any improvements now. The universe is finished; the copestone is on, and the chips were carted off a million years ago. Poor Lazarus there, chattering his teeth against the curbstone for his pillow, and shaking off his tatters with his shivering — he might plug up both ears with rags and put a corncob in his mouth, and still that would not keep out the tempestuous Euroclydon. Euroclydon! says old Dives, in his red silk robe (he had a redder one afterward) — pooh, pooh! What a fine frosty night; how Orion glitters; what northern lights! Let them talk of their Eastern summer climates of everlasting conservatories; give me the privilege of making my own summer with my own coals.

items.new: Entering that gable-ended Spouter-Inn, you found yourself in a wide, low, straggling entry with old-fashioned wood paneling, reminding you of the bulwarks of some condemned old ship. On one side hung a very large oil painting so thoroughly blackened by smoke, and defaced in every way, that in the uneven crosslights by which you viewed it, it was only by diligent study, a series of systematic visits, and careful inquiry of the neighbors that you could arrive at any understanding of its purpose. There were such unaccountable masses of shades and shadows that at first you almost thought some ambitious young artist, in the time of the New England witches, had tried to depict chaos bewitched. But by dint of much earnest contemplation and oft-repeated pondering, and especially by throwing open the little window toward the back of the entry, you at last came to the conclusion that such an idea, however wild, might not be altogether unwarranted.

items.new: But what most puzzled and confounded you was a long, limber, portentous, black mass of something hovering in the center of the picture over three blue, dim, perpendicular lines floating in a nameless yeast. A boggy, soggy, squelchy picture truly, enough to drive a nervous man to distraction. Yet there was a sort of indefinite, half-attained, unimaginable sublimity about it that fairly froze you to it, until you involuntarily swore an oath to yourself to find out what that marvelous painting meant. Every now and then a bright but, alas, deceptive idea would dart through you. — It's the Black Sea in a midnight gale. — It's the unnatural combat of the four primal elements. — It's a blasted heath. — It's a Hyperborean winter scene, from the far frozen north. — It's the breaking-up of the icebound stream of Time. But at last all these fancies yielded to that one portentous something in the middle of the picture. Once that was found out, all the rest would be plain. But wait; doesn't it bear a faint resemblance to a gigantic fish? Even the great leviathan himself?

items.new: The opposite wall of this entry was hung all over with a heathenish array of monstrous clubs and spears. Some were thickly set with glittering teeth resembling ivory saws; others were tufted with knots of human hair; and one was sickle-shaped, with a vast handle sweeping around like the curve a long-armed mower cuts in new-mown grass. You shuddered as you gazed, and wondered what monstrous cannibal and savage could ever have gone death-harvesting with such a hacking, horrifying implement. Mixed with these were rusty old whaling lances and harpoons, all broken and deformed. Some were storied weapons. With this once-long lance, now wildly bent at the elbow, Nathan Swain killed fifteen whales between one sunrise and sunset fifty years ago. And that harpoon — so like a corkscrew now — was thrown in Javan seas, and run away with by a whale that was killed years afterward off the Cape of Blanco. The original iron entered near the tail and, like a restless needle wandering around in the body of a man, traveled a full forty feet, and at last was found embedded in the hump.

items.new: Crossing this dusky entry, and going on through that low-arched way — cut through what in old times must have been a great central chimney with fireplaces all around — you enter the public room. This is an even duskier place, with such low, ponderous beams above and such old wrinkled planks beneath that you would almost imagine you were treading some old ship's cockpits, especially on such a howling night, when this corner-anchored old ark rocked so furiously. On one side stood a long, low, shelf-like table covered with cracked glass cases, filled with dusty rarities gathered from the remotest nooks of this wide world. Projecting from the farther corner of the room stands a dark-looking den — the bar — a crude attempt at a right whale's head. Be that as it may, there stands the vast arched bone of the whale's jaw, so wide that a coach might almost drive beneath it. Inside are shabby shelves lined with old decanters, bottles, and flasks; and in those jaws of swift destruction, like another cursed Jonah (which indeed is what they called him), bustles a little withered old man who, for their money, sells the sailors delirium and death at a dear price.

This man interested me at once; and since the sea-gods had ordained that he should soon become my shipmate (though only a sleeping-partner one, as far as this narrative is concerned), I will venture a little description of him here. He stood a full six feet tall, with noble shoulders and a chest like a coffer-dam. I have seldom seen such brawn in a man. His face was deeply browned and sunburnt, which made his white teeth dazzling by contrast; while in the deep shadows of his eyes floated some memories that did not seem to give him much joy. His voice at once announced that he was a Southerner, and from his fine stature I thought he must be one of those tall mountaineers from the Alleghanian Ridge in Virginia. When the revelry of his companions had reached its height, this man slipped away unobserved, and I saw no more of him until he became my comrade on the sea. items.new: Nobody prefers to sleep two in a bed. In fact, you would much rather not sleep with your own brother. I don't know how it is, but people like to be private when they are sleeping. And when it comes to sleeping with an unknown stranger, in a strange inn, in a strange town — and that stranger a harpooner — then your objections multiply indefinitely. items.new: Lord save me, I thought, that must be the harpooner, the infernal head-peddler. But I lay perfectly still, and resolved not to say a word until spoken to. Holding a light in one hand, and that same New Zealand head in the other, the stranger entered the room and, without looking toward the bed, placed his candle a good way off from me on the floor in one corner, and then began working away at the knotted cords of the large bag I mentioned before as being in the room. I was all eagerness to see his face, but he kept it turned away for some time while busy unlacing the bag's mouth. This done, however, he turned around — when, good heavens! What a sight! Such a face! It was of a dark, purplish, yellow color, stuck over here and there with large blackish-looking squares. Yes, it's just as I thought: he's a terrible bedfellow; he's been in a fight, got dreadfully cut, and here he is, just back from the surgeon. But at that moment he happened to turn his face toward the light in such a way that I plainly saw those black squares on his cheeks could not be sticking-plasters at all. They were stains of some sort or other. At first I didn't know what to make of this; but soon an inkling of the truth occurred to me. I remembered a story of a white man — a whaleman, too — who, falling among the cannibals, had been tattooed by them. I concluded that this harpooner, in the course of his distant voyages, must have met with a similar adventure. And what is it, after all, I thought! It's only his outside; a man can be honest in any sort of skin. But then, what to make of his unearthly complexion — the part of it, I mean, lying round about, and completely independent of, the squares of tattooing? To be sure, it might be nothing but a good coat of tropical tanning; but I never heard of a hot sun tanning a white man into a purplish yellow one. However, I had never been in the South Seas; and perhaps the sun there produced these extraordinary effects on the skin. Now, while all these ideas were passing through me like lightning, this harpooner never noticed me at all. But after some difficulty in opening his bag, he began fumbling in it, and soon pulled out a sort of tomahawk and a sealskin wallet with the hair still on. Placing these on the old chest in the middle of the room, he then took the New Zealand head — a ghastly enough thing — and crammed it down into the bag. He now took off his hat — a new beaver hat — when I came near crying out with fresh surprise. There was no hair on his head — none to speak of, at least — nothing but a small scalp-knot twisted up on his forehead. His bald purplish head now looked for all the world like a mildewed skull. If the stranger had not stood between me and the door, I would have bolted out of it quicker than I ever bolted a dinner.

items.new: My sensations were strange. Let me try to explain them. When I was a child, I well remember, something somewhat similar happened to me — whether it was real or a dream, I could never entirely settle. It was this. I had been up to some mischief or other — I think it was trying to crawl up the chimney, as I had seen a little chimney sweep do a few days before; and my stepmother, who somehow or other was always whipping me or sending me to bed without supper — my mother dragged me by the legs out of the chimney and packed me off to bed, though it was only two o'clock in the afternoon of the 21st of June, the longest day of the year in our hemisphere. items.new: I lay there dismally calculating that sixteen entire hours must pass before I could hope for a resurrection. Sixteen hours in bed! The small of my back ached to think of it. And it was so light, too — the sun shining in at the window, a great rattling of coaches in the streets, and the sound of cheerful voices all over the house. I felt worse and worse. At last I got up, dressed, and, going softly downstairs in my stocking feet, sought out my stepmother and suddenly threw myself at her feet, begging her as a particular favor to give me a good slippering for my misbehavior — anything, indeed, but condemning me to lie in bed for such an unendurable length of time. But she was the best and most conscientious of stepmothers, and back I had to go to my room. For several hours I lay there wide awake, feeling a great deal worse than I have ever felt since, even from the greatest later misfortunes. At last I must have fallen into a troubled nightmare of a doze; and slowly waking from it — half steeped in dreams — I opened my eyes, and the room that had been sunlit was now wrapped in outer darkness. Instantly I felt a shock run through my whole frame; nothing was to be seen, and nothing was to be heard; but a supernatural hand seemed placed in mine. My arm hung over the counterpane, and the nameless, unimaginable, silent form or phantom to which the hand belonged seemed to be sitting close by my bedside. For what seemed ages piled on ages, I lay there, frozen with the most awful fears, not daring to drag my hand away, yet always thinking that if I could only stir it one single inch, the horrid spell would be broken. I don't know how this awareness at last slipped away from me; but waking in the morning, I shudderingly remembered it all, and for days and weeks and months afterward I lost myself in bewildering attempts to explain the mystery. Indeed, to this very hour, I often puzzle over it.

items.new: Now, take away the awful fear, and my sensations at feeling the supernatural hand in mine were very similar, in their strangeness, to those I experienced on waking up and seeing Queequeg's pagan arm thrown around me. But at length all the events of the past night soberly came back, one by one, in fixed reality, and then I was alive only to the comical predicament. For though I tried to move his arm — to unlock his bridegroom clasp — yet, sleeping as he was, he still hugged me tightly, as though nothing but death should part us two. I now tried to rouse him — "Queequeg!" — but his only answer was a snore. I then rolled over, my neck feeling as if it were in a horse collar, and suddenly felt a slight scratch. Throwing aside the counterpane, there lay the tomahawk sleeping by the savage's side, as if it were a hatchet-faced baby. A pretty pickle, truly, I thought; in bed here in a strange house in broad daylight, with a cannibal and a tomahawk! "Queequeg! In the name of goodness, Queequeg, wake up!" At length, by dint of much wriggling, and loud and incessant protests about the unseemliness of his hugging a fellow male in that matrimonial sort of style, I succeeded in extracting a grunt; and presently he drew back his arm, shook himself all over like a Newfoundland dog just out of the water, and sat up in bed, stiff as a pikestaff, looking at me and rubbing his eyes as if he did not altogether remember how I came to be there, though a dim awareness of knowing something about me seemed slowly to be dawning over him. Meanwhile, I lay quietly eyeing him, having no serious misgivings now, and intent on closely observing so curious a creature. When at last his mind seemed made up about the character of his bedfellow, and he had become, as it were, reconciled to the fact, he jumped out onto the floor, and by certain signs and sounds gave me to understand that, if I liked, he would dress first and then leave me to dress afterward, leaving the whole room to myself. Queequeg, I thought, under the circumstances this is a very civilized overture; but the truth is, these savages have an innate sense of delicacy, say what you will; it is marvelous how essentially polite they are. I pay this particular compliment to Queequeg because he treated me with so much civility and consideration, while I was guilty of great rudeness — staring at him from the bed and watching all his dressing motions, my curiosity for the time getting the better of my upbringing. Still, a man like Queequeg you don't see every day; he and his ways were well worth unusual attention.

items.new: He began dressing at the top by putting on his beaver hat — a very tall one, by the way — and then, still without his trousers, he hunted up his boots. What under heaven he did it for, I can't tell, but his next move was to crush himself — boots in hand and hat on — under the bed; and from various violent gaspings and strainings, I inferred he was hard at work booting himself, though by no law of propriety that I ever heard of is any man required to be private when putting on his boots. But Queequeg, you see, was a creature in the transition stage — neither caterpillar nor butterfly. He was just civilized enough to show off his outlandishness in the strangest possible ways. His education was not yet complete. He was an undergraduate. If he had not been a little civilized, he very probably would not have bothered himself with boots at all; but then, if he had not still been a savage, he would never have dreamed of getting under the bed to put them on. At last he emerged with his hat badly dented and crushed down over his eyes, and began creaking and limping about the room, as if, not being much used to boots, his pair of damp, wrinkled cowhide ones — probably not made to order, either — rather pinched and tormented him at the start of a bitter cold morning.

items.new: Seeing now that there were no curtains on the window, and that, the street being very narrow, the house opposite had a plain view into the room, and noticing more and more what an indecent figure Queequeg made, stomping about with little else on but his hat and boots, I begged him as well as I could to hurry his dressing somewhat, and especially to get into his trousers as soon as possible. He complied, and then proceeded to wash himself. At that time in the morning any Christian would have washed his face; but Queequeg, to my amazement, was content to restrict his washing to his chest, arms, and hands. He then put on his waistcoat, and, picking up a piece of hard soap from the washstand center table, dipped it in water and began lathering his face. I was watching to see where he kept his razor, when lo and behold, he takes the harpoon from the bed corner, slips off the long wooden shaft, unsheathes the head, whets it a little on his boot, and, striding up to the bit of mirror against the wall, begins a vigorous scraping — or rather harpooning — of his cheeks. Queequeg, I thought, this is using Rogers's best cutlery with a vengeance. Afterward I wondered less at this operation, when I came to know what fine steel the head of a harpoon is made of, and how extremely sharp its long straight edges are always kept.

items.new: These reflections are prompted just here by the fact that after we were all seated at the table, and I was preparing to hear some good stories about whaling, to my no small surprise nearly every man kept a profound silence. And not only that, but they looked embarrassed. Yes, here was a set of sea dogs, many of whom had, without the slightest bashfulness, boarded great whales on the high seas — entire strangers to them — and dueled them dead without blinking; and yet here they sat at a social breakfast table — all of the same calling, all of kindred tastes — looking around at each other as sheepishly as though they had never been out of sight of some sheepfold among the Green Mountains. A curious sight — these bashful bears, these timid warrior whalemen!
